review_text_raw:
I did really enjoy this game. It is very story-driven, and does involve a lot of reading - which I don't mind - but if you do this game won't be for you. I've played through once, took me about 2 1/2 - 3 hours, however I didn't fully read every article, I mostly just scanned through looking for data.
The game scared me, scared me to know that people do this in real life, and at points I was so into the story that I felt like I was actually spying on people. 
I don't know whether choices matter in this game, some parts (especially the ending) seemed to suggest so, if it does that would make the game better, if not, I believe that should be in there - this would work great as a choices matter. The ending did confuse me, which also suggested that choices matter, but I require further playthrough before doing so.

Overall, this is a good game, and I would recommend if you like a very story-driven experience!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.
However, Orwell is far better experienced (in my opinion) to just "do" and let the events unfold.

But as I said, if you are anxious about making the wrong call, you might not enjoy this game.
If you are neither scared by that nor by "this-isn't-a-game"-sayers, then you might really enjoy this game. I picked it up at a sale and enjoyed my time with it - hopefully you will too.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts. [h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2] Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that. [h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2] The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%. Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch! My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements. For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! [h1] Overall Rating [/h1] [b] WIP, FIS, IIS 2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Given all the positive reviews, I thought Orwell would be a more interesting game than it actually is.
But the gameplay is mostly boring. In a way, it is very similar to a text-adventure game. You read through/listen to all the documents given access to (webpages, chat sessions or phone calls). But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Except most of the info you have to read through is about the different suspects boring life, relationships and habits, things I don't give a damn about. So I guess this game is not for me.

Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

- Engaging ethical themes and dilemmas
- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

review_text_raw:
I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the core concept is interesting, the game play and plot leave much to be desired. It is also incredibly short. The TLDR is that I would not recommend this unless the concept really grabs you.

The story revolves around a bombing and the activist group linked to it. You take the role of an investigator using social media, private messages/files and recorded phone calls to get to the bottom of everything. There seem to be a few possible different outcomes which could be interesting to explore if the people involved weren't so... stupid. I wont spoil anything but they basically make their own problems and then make bigger problems for themselves because they incorrectly think the bigger problems will solve their problems. It's like watching a train wreck in slow motion. It can be hard to get invested when you can't relate or empathise with the characters. I found myself thinking that most of them were horrible people who deserved what the plot threw at them.

The game play consists of reading through documents and chat logs and dragging over information that you determine to be relevant to the case. Some of this information is incorrect or contradictory and so you must vet information before committing it to the system. There are no taking information back even if you find contradicting information later on. This means a lot of your time will be spent going back and forward between different documents to pick out information and drag it to the appropriate file. This isn't exactly the most invigorating game play but when you are in the zone it can be somewhat enjoyable.

There isn't really much else to say. The game does have a political agenda and a underlying moral to it but it kind of falls on its face to the extent that I started to wonder if the resistant reading was the intended one.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]

review_text_raw:
I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

This NSA reading simulator is actually kind of a fun little game. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
My intention was to write this review after completing the fifth and final chapter after its release. Now that I've completed the game, I feel that I can give this game the review that it deserves. 

I was very, very surprised with how well this game was executed. I've never come across a game quite like this. Orwell is a game where you play as an investigator who is trying to discover the person behind a crime by ruffling through relevant internet posts as well as phone calls, emails, etc. You then send information you deem as relevant to your advisor, who then decides what to do with said information. As I was playing this game, I really felt the pressure on what kind of narrative I was showing to the government and the policeforce regarding the people I was investigating, which is why I believe this game is so brilliant. You really feel the need to think carefully about what things you send out because there is no taking back what you submit once it's out there, which I believe is one of the underlying messages of the game's story. 

I would liken this game to an interactive choose-your-own adventure. Regarding the gameplay, it does not involve much other than reading through files and articles, and clicking to drag data of your choice into the government's database. Certain pieces of information will unlock more articles and files for you to read through. That being said, while I was playing the game these simple mechanics actually helped me stay more immersed in the story. They were uncomplicated and helped my attention stay focused on my "job" and the impact I was having. If your idea of a good game involves more gameplay elements than this, I would not recommend it to you, but if you really enjoy a good story, then please consider giving this game a try. 

Where this game really thrives, I believe, is its attention to detail. The writing in this game is fantastic, as well as the music. The music is mainly ambient, but when you come across important information the music changes dramatically to match the feeling of what you have discovered. The writing paired with the music really kept me at the edge of my seat throughout each episode. I really enjoyed how versatile the writing was as well. The writers managed to create incredibly in-depth characters that each felt very real with their own motives and personalities. At times I felt obligated to protect these people or felt awful about info I might have uploaded about them if it turned out I was incorrect. Without spoiling anything, the writing really makes you think about how people generally show many different aspects of themselves to different people, and as the investigator you have to decipher which "mask" is the way that person really feels or thinks. 

Unfortunately for people who buy the game at this point, you will not be getting the weekly emails to report back to duty  because all five episodes have already been released. These emails really helped me stay immersed in the universe of the game and I really felt like I was reporting back to duty for a job, and I commend the developers for these small touches that added to my immersion in the game. Even though players who buy the game now have access to all episodes at once, I would really recommend taking a break of a day between each episode if you can. I really think it will help you stay immersed in the world. 

Honestly, if you enjoy dystopian stories like 1984 and want to experience an innovative way of playing, you will really enjoy this game. I hope that many people give this game a chance because it will really make you question government security and the things that you post publicly online. I'm going to keep an eye out for more games by these developers because I feel that they are really creating a new, innovative market and I am really excited to see what else they can bring to the gaming industry. 

I give this game a 10/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

It was fun, but definitely deserves to be played with time and clear mind.

Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an narrative game with unique gameplay. The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator whose job it is to keep the Nation safe. You work with the titular program 'Orwell' which is an advanced search engine that lets you browse the in game internet in search of terrorists. You will start of by reading through public blogs, forums and social media. But as the stakes rise and the public information dries up you will find yourself spending more and more time eavesdropping on phone calls and hacking into personal files.

The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Deus Ex. I personally loved hacking computers and reading emails in those games, and Orwell turns this side activity into a full game. This means that you will do a lot of reading, although the useable pieces of information are always highlighted. You can upload these 'data chunks' to your superior, who will act on the information you feed him. Your superior cannot read anything except for the parts you upload, which gives you the freedom to interpret the data and even 'spin' it. Do you focus on the information that marks someone as potentially dangerous or do you focus on their peaceful side? This will ofcourse have consequences down the road.

Speaking of consequences, these are actually real in this game. Although your actions will not change the core structure of the narrative, they will have a very clear impact. All suspects can be arrested, one can be killed, or you can let them all go free. What makes this game unique is that most consequences are not directly tied to a single choice, but to a whole set of smaller decisions. There is no 'do you let this person live?' moment. Instead the choices you made in what data you upload and what information you ignore will determine the fate of the characters. The ending may appear to be a 'choose your own ending' affair at first, but a replay made it clear to me that your earlier choices will still impact the ending you get.

The theme of the game is privacy vs safety. But unlike other games or media on this subject, there is no clear black or white. The game shows that your work can save lives, but that it also has the potential to ruin them. The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves.

Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second.

There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day.

Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

review_text_raw: In the first 3 episodes I was very interested and engaged in the story but after that I got very disengaged and bored. Partly because of the constant clicking and dragging but also because it felt like the dialogue sections were becoming longer and more dragged out the more I progressed. Don't get me wrong, this game has a very interesting and thought provoking story and if you enjoy story rich cinematic games this game might be right up your alley. However, personally I felt that the game play got quite repetitive and tedious after a while, and some dialogue (particularly the last one) were just way too long and slow for me to be able to stay engaged and pay attention to throughout. I really wish you were able to skip ahead and just read through them yourself or speed them up even more than possible, instead of having to wait for each response from each person.

I just got through chapter 3. I bought it blind on sale last winter sale.

It's an amazing interactive story when it comes down to it. Has some clever nods to 1984 by Orwell (a little obviously by premise) but little details that make the nods a little more important. Is this a game for everyone? No. It has a lot of reading but if you don't mind that it's very interesting in premise and storytelling. 

Over all a solid 6/10 if you don't like reading
9.5/10 if you enjoy reading

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
*TL;DR AT BOTTOM* 
Firstly I'd just like to say I'm not one to review games often, but I'll give it a shot. I'll give a little overview of my view, a summary of how the game works, some of the pros, the cons, who I'd recommend the game for, and then a final rating.

So I've just finished playing through one run of the game, well doing one run through of it and I have to say I've really enjoyed it. It's incredibly well designed, with a brilliant branching storyline which you have a direct effect on. Admittedly it only has a few hours of playing if you only want to do the one run through, but if you're even more of a completionist than I am there is some replayablity, as the different choices you make influence the development of the situation, who gets arrested, who is charged with what, through to the political outcomes.

Basically the game focuses on a network of people who are implicated after a bomb goes off, and you play the role of an investigator, who has the job of going through various news sources, private files, phone calls, social media communications etc, and choosing what datachunks to process, in order to solve the various tasks you are presented with. Sometimes you might face conflicting bits of data, and it's down to you to choose what to process, this can be based on ignorant sources, or particular context of the sources. 

As mentioned, the storyline that you can influence is particularly interesting, and the general depth to the characters and plot is quite phenomenal. The game itself runs very easily, and though overall you are a little guided with what to look at, this fits with the overall design of the surveillance system you are a part of. I particularly like the flexibility you have, in that if you want you can be like me and just read through loads of different material which might not even help you, but can immerse you in the setting. Further, there were one or two moments where I was wondering what should I do next, but as it all turned out I had overlooked or forgot about particular things, so it's not too complex, but does require a little thought.

In terms of negatives, there's not too much to complain about. In terms of the game, maybe the ability to load up the game on the different days or after each task is done, particularly towards the end of the story, would be good, in order to just look at the different endings without a full replay. I loved the story, and look forward to playing the next game, but I still would have loved if the game had been longer. Which brings me to the price, at £7.19, for only 4 hours content (well for me anyway with only one run through), the game might be a little steep, but I really enjoyed it to be honest, and if you see it in a sale, go for it.

Overall I'm going to say the game itself is a 9/10, very well designed, but the experience as a whole is more a 7/10 due to the limited playtime for the price. Long review for sure, but hope it helped. Enjoy your day!

TL;DR: Well designed game with branching/influenceable story, deep setting, drawing on relevant themes with surveillance, government, and freedom vs security, unique game type, quite a price for relatively short amount of playtime, deffo worth on sale, 9/10 game itself, 7/10 factoring in price and content.
